Introduction:
According to the World Health Organization, harmful use of alcohol is a leading cause of poor health and premature death globally [ 1 ]. On a global basis, deaths attributable to alcohol intake include deaths due to chronic diseases such as cancer (4.8%) and cardiovascular disease (3.2%) [ 2 ]. Observational studies have also suggested a lower risk of ischaemic heart disease [ 3 , 4 ], ischaemic stroke [ 5 ] and death from these [ 6–8 ] with low levels of alcohol intake in the absence of heavy episodic drinking, compared with abstention. The validity of these findings is not universally accepted [ 9 ], as these studies classify individuals who have given up drinking due to poor health (‘sick quitters’) within the reference population of non-drinkers [ 10 , 11 ]. In addition, cohort studies assessing the association between alcohol intake and mortality have predominantly measured intake close to study enrolment [ 12 ], usually during middle age, or have used a summary measure of cumulative lifetime intake [ 13 , 14 ], although intake is likely to vary over the life course [ 15 , 16 ]. As a consequence, these studies fail to capture adverse mortality effects from more complex patterns of alcohol intake over time.

In the present study, we aimed to minimize limitations of published work by identifying long-term drinking trajectories over the life course using retrospectively collected intake data at various age periods before enrolment in a cohort study, and we examined associations with all-cause, cardiovascular disease-specific, and cancer-specific mortality.
Methods:
### Participants

The Melbourne Collaborative Cohort Study (MCCS) is a prospective study of 41 513 people (58.9% women; 99.2% aged 40–69 years) recruited during 1990–94 in Melbourne, Australia [ 17 ]. The Cancer Council Victoria Human Research Ethics Committee approved the study protocol. We excluded participants aged <40 or ≥70 years ( n = 325) at recruitment, with missing lifetime alcohol intake data ( n = 399) or reporting alcohol intake for fewer than three decades of life ( n = 2), with extreme values of total energy intake (<1st percentile and >99th percentile) ( n = 807) or with missing data on any of the covariates modelled ( n = 392), leaving 39 588 (95.4% of the total cohort; 23 527 women and 16 061 men) for analysis ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ).

### Collection of data

Information on demographics and potential risk factors, including lifestyle behaviours, was collected using structured questionnaires at study entry in 1990–94. A 121-item food frequency questionnaire was used to collect dietary information [ 18 ], and height and weight were measured.

### Assessment of alcohol intake

Participants were asked at baseline if they had ever drunk at least 12 alcoholic drinks in a year. Those who answered yes (‘non-lifetime abstainers’) were then asked about their usual frequency of consumption and usual quantity consumed per drinking occasion for beer, wine, and spirits separately during 10-year age periods commencing at age 20 years, up to the decade of their age at baseline attendance. We calculated the usual intake within each age period in grams per day for each beverage type by multiplying intake frequency by quantity and standard amount of alcohol per container using data from Australian food composition tables [ 19 ]. The alcohol intake for each age period in grams per day was calculated as the sum of intake from the three beverage types. The alcohol intake for the age decade encompassing baseline was considered the intake at baseline age. The average lifetime alcohol intake in grams per day was derived by dividing the total lifetime intake by the total number of days within the age intervals up to study enrolment [ 20 ].

### Cohort follow-up and ascertainment of deaths

Deaths were identified from the Victorian Cancer Registry and the Victorian Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages up to 30 June 2021. Information on cause of death was obtained up to 31 October 2018 (99% complete). The cause of death was classified as cardiovascular [410–414 and 430–438 for the 9th revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-9); I20–I25 and I60–I69 for the 10th revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10)], cancer (140–239 for ICD-9 and C00–C97 for ICD-10), or due to other causes (including 1% missing cause of death).

### Alcohol intake trajectories

Clusters of individuals following similar long-term sex-specific alcohol intake trajectories from age 20 years to baseline were identified using a semiparametric group-based trajectory model. This model is an application of finite mixture modelling, which assumes the study sample is composed of a mixture of groups following homogenous courses [ 21 ]. Sex-specific longitudinal alcohol intake data were fitted as a mixture of several latent trajectories in a censored normal model, allowing for the lower (zero g/day) and upper intake (capped at 100 g/day; <2% of men and <0.2% of women had intakes of >100 g/day at each age decade) limits, with a polynomial function for age [ 21 , 22 ]. A two-step modelling process was used where we first selected the optimal number of trajectories and then determined the optimal shape of these trajectories using the Bayesian information criterion and an approximation of the log Bayes factor [ 21 , 23 ]. Approximately 30% of MCCS participants had never drunk alcohol or had very low intakes (<0.5 g/day) over the observation period, so in the first step, we included a zero-order (or constant) trajectory and selected five more groups as quadratic functions of age. Next, we determined the preferred order of the polynomial (i.e. constant, linear, quadratic, or cubic) for each trajectory. Participants were assigned to the group for which their posterior predicted probability calculated from the final model was highest. The adequacy of the fit of the final model was evaluated using recommended diagnostic measures: average posterior probability of assignment for each group of 0.7 or higher; odds of correct classification of 5.0 or higher; the proportion of the sample assigned to a certain group close to the proportion estimated from the model; and a reasonably narrow confidence interval (CI) around each trajectory. Alcohol intakes reported by each participant for each 10-year age period preceding their age decade at baseline attendance were considered intakes at the start of those age decades, and intake reported for the decade of age at baseline attendance was used as their intake at baseline age.

### Statistical analyses

We used Cox regression [ 24 ] to estimate hazard ratios (HR) and 95% CIs for associations with all-cause mortality and disease-specific mortality, with age as the time metric. Follow-up began at baseline attendance and ended at the earlier of the date of death or the end of follow-up (30 June 2021 for all-cause mortality and 31 October 2018 for disease-specific deaths). To estimate HRs for cardiovascular disease-specific and cancer-specific mortality, Cox regression models were fit using a data duplication competing risks method [ 25 ], which also included competing deaths due to other causes. We fit interaction terms to test for differences in associations by smoking status (never vs current/former), a potential effect modifier. We compared findings for alcohol intake trajectories with the HRs obtained for lifetime and baseline alcohol intake (women: abstention; >0–19; 20–39; and ≥40 g/day; men: abstention; >0–19; 20–39; 40–59; 60–79; and ≥80 g/day).

A causal diagram and existing evidence guided the inclusion of confounding variables [ 26 ] (all measured at baseline, at the last alcohol assessment) in multivariable models. Alcohol intake was modelled as sex-specific trajectories in models adjusted for education, socioeconomic status, household size, smoking status, fruit intake, vegetable intake, physical activity [ 27 ], body mass index (BMI), energy from food, saturated fat intake, and stratified by birth cohort and country of birth. Excess body fatness might be a consequence rather than a cause of alcohol consumption. Therefore, we fitted models with and without adjustment for BMI. We considered the model with adjustment for BMI to be the primary analysis.

Sensitivity analyses were performed excluding the first 2 years of follow-up to account for potential reverse causation and with models adjusted for Mediterranean diet score [ 28 ] instead of fruit, vegetable, and saturated fat intake. Each model was examined for outliers and influential points. Nested models were compared using the likelihood ratio test [ 29 ]. Tests based on Schoenfeld residuals were used to examine the proportional hazards assumption [ 30 ]. Cox models assessing overall mortality were stratified on smoking status and household size (men only) as there was evidence of non-proportional hazards for these variables. All statistical tests were two-sided, and statistical analyses were performed using Stata 16.1 (StataCorp, College Station, TX).
Results:
There were 7664 deaths in women during 595 456 person-years of follow-up (mean 25.3 person-years) and 7132 deaths in men during 377 314 person-years of follow-up (mean 23.5 person-years). There were 1117 (14.6%) deaths due to cardiovascular disease and 2251 (29.4%) due to cancer in women and 1283 (18.0%) cardiovascular deaths and 2340 (32.8%) cancer deaths in men.

We identified six trajectories (TR) of lifetime alcohol intake for men and three for women ( Fig. 1 ). Lifetime abstention (classified as TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’) was selected as the reference category and included 39% of the women (99.7% of whom had never consumed alcohol over their lifetime and maximum mean <1.0 g/day at each data point for the other 0.3%) and 14% of the men (99.5% of whom had never consumed alcohol over their lifetime and maximum mean <1.0 g/day at each data point for the other 0.5%). Most men (72%; TR2 ‘stable light’, TR3 ‘stable moderate’) and women (54%; TR2 ‘stable light’) had relatively stable alcohol intake over their lifetime; 6%–7% of men and women tended to increase their alcohol intake across the lifespan (men: classified as TR4 ‘increasing heavy’ who reported a mean intake of 36–55 g/day at age 20–39 years but increased their alcohol intake markedly over time, consuming over 60 g/day from age 40–49 years before reducing their intake by age 60–69 years; women: classified as TR3 ‘increasing moderate’ who tended to consume around 22 g/day at age 20–29 years but gradually increased their alcohol intake over time to consume close to 40 g/day at age 50–59 years). The heavy drinkers among men at age 20–39 years (mean intake ≥60 g/day) tended to either cut down their intake from age 40–49 years and had lower mean intakes compared with TR2 ‘stable light’ drinkers by age 60–69 years (5.4%; TR5 ‘early decreasing heavy’) or continued to drink heavily until age 60–69 years before cutting down their intake, but still remained heavy drinkers at age 60–69 years (2.1%; TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’).

Out of the men with intake data for age 60–69 years, 55% classified as TR5 ‘early decreasing heavy’ had quit drinking by age 60 years compared with 13% classified as TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’. The drinking trajectories remained relatively consistent across participants aged 40–49, 50–59, and 60–69 years at study enrolment ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Sex-specific model adequacy diagnostics are presented in Supplementary Table S1 and characteristics of participants by alcohol intake trajectories in Table 1 .

### Alcohol intake trajectories and all-cause mortality

For both women and men, stable intake trajectories were associated with lower overall mortality (women: TR2 ‘stable light’ HR 0.91; 95% CI 0.87–0.96; men: TR2 ‘stable light’ HR 0.88; 95% CI 0.82–0.94 and TR3 ‘stable moderate’ HR 0.88; 95% CI 0.81–0.96), compared with TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’ ( Table 2 ). For men, relative to TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’, heavy intake trajectories were associated with higher overall mortality (TR5 ‘early decreasing heavy’ HR 1.18; 95% CI 1.05–1.32; TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’ HR 1.21; 95% CI 1.04–1.40) ( Table 2 ). HRs for TR3 ‘increasing moderate’ for women and TR4 ‘increasing heavy’ for men were not suggestive of associations with all-cause mortality. The strength of these associations did not vary appreciably according to smoking status ( P interaction > .5) except for the weakening of associations for TR3 ‘stable moderate’ and TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’ for never smoking men ( Supplementary Table S2 ).

### Alcohol intake trajectories and disease-specific mortality

An association between stable intake, relative to TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’, and lower cardiovascular disease-specific mortality was limited to TR2 ‘stable light’ for men (HR 0.83; 95% CI 0.71–0.97). Only weak inverse associations were observed for TR2 ‘stable light’ for women and TR3 ‘stable moderate’ for men, relative to TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’, and lower cardiovascular disease-specific mortality (HR 0.90; 95% CI 0.79–1.02 and HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.70–1.01, respectively) ( Table 3 ).

For women, 19% higher cancer-specific mortality for TR3 ‘increasing moderate’ (HR 1.19; 95% CI 1.00–1.43), and for men, 34%–37% higher cancer-specific mortality for TR5 ‘early decreasing heavy’ (HR 1.34; 95% CI 1.10–1.64) and TR6 ‘late decreasing heavy’ (HR 1.37; 95% CI 1.06–1.77), compared with TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’, were observed; the 95% CIs included the null for cardiovascular disease-specific mortality (for these groups for men) ( Table 3 ).

For men, TR4 ‘increasing heavy’ demonstrated lower cardiovascular disease-specific mortality (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.61–1.01) and higher cancer-specific mortality (HR 1.16; 95% CI 0.97–1.39), compared with TR1 ‘lifetime abstention’, although the strength of the association was weak ( Table 3 ).

### Lifetime and baseline alcohol intake and mortality

The associations between usual lifetime and baseline alcohol intake and overall and disease-specific mortality are shown in Table 4 . Positive associations were limited to all-cause mortality for the heaviest-drinking men for lifetime and baseline intake and to cancer-specific mortality for the heaviest-drinking women and men for lifetime intake.

### Sensitivity analyses

The sex-specific results from the analysis excluding the first 2 years of follow-up, without adjusting for BMI or adjusting for Mediterranean diet score were not materially different from the main results ( Supplementary Tables S3–S5 ). Models including alcohol-intake trajectories showed overall better model fit in comparison to models using lifetime or baseline intake ( Supplementary Table S6 ).
Discussion:
Compared with lifetime abstention, stable light and moderate drinking were associated with ∼10% lower all-cause mortality for women and men, largely attributable to lower cardiovascular disease mortality. Heavy drinking during early adulthood for men, irrespective of intake after age 40 years, was associated with ∼20% higher all-cause mortality and 35% higher cancer-specific mortality, while increasing alcohol intake with advancing age for women was associated with ∼20% higher cancer-specific mortality.

Strengths of our study include the detailed assessment of alcohol intake over the life course and the long follow-up. There are several limitations. Alcohol intake was self-reported, which is prone to measurement error. For example, studies using data from surveys asking about frequency and amount of consumption of different alcoholic beverages in the last year have typically found coverage rates (comparing self-reported drinking and data from production, sales, trade, and tax records in a population) of <50% [ 31 ]. Intake at baseline may have influenced their recall of past alcohol intake, while misclassification due to participants having to summarize their frequency and quantity of alcoholic beverage intake for 10-year age intervals into single ‘usual’ values is also possible. According to Rehm et al. [ 32 ] measuring intake both at a point in time (e.g. at baseline) and over a period of time (e.g. during lifetime) helps limit problems related to intake measurement. We previously established the accuracy of recalled alcohol intake data in the MCCS by comparing matching temporal changes in intake over time for study participants with Australian per capita trends. However, it is still possible that drinking trajectories in the MCCS may not fully represent recent drinking rates in Australia, particularly for women [ 33 ].

Cancer is the second-leading cause of death due to alcohol use in Australia. Globally, 740 000 new cancer cases [ 34 ] and 400 000 cancer deaths each year are attributed to drinking [ 35 ]. In the present study, heavy drinking during different age periods in women and men was related to higher cancer-specific mortality. Acetaldehyde, the toxic metabolite of ethanol in alcoholic beverages, is a carcinogen [ 36 ] causally linked to cancers of the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, oesophagus (squamous-cell carcinoma), liver, colorectum, and female breast [ 37 ]. Several of these cancers remain among the most lethal cancers, with median survival <1 year [ 38 , 39 ]. Two key findings in our study merit further examination in future research: (i) men who drank heavily in their 20s and 30s were at higher risk of death by middle age even when most had quit by then; and (ii) women with markedly lower intake compared with men were at higher risk of cancer-specific mortality in their middle age. These findings emphasise the potential relevance of age and sex when formulating national drinking guidelines. The current Australian guidelines on reducing health risks from drinking alcohol advocate that healthy men and women should drink no more than 10 standard drinks a week and no more than 4 standard drinks on any 1 day [ 40 ]. In comparison, the Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend limiting intake to two drinks or less in a day for men and one drink or less in a day for women, on days when alcohol is consumed, and avoiding binge drinking.

In the present study, in line with published data [ 14 , 41 ], we identified a relatively small mortality benefit for stable light and stable moderate drinking due to lower cardiovascular disease-specific mortality, particularly for men. In a comparatively smaller study employing group-based trajectory modelling, four long-term drinking patterns were identified in 5298 Chinese women and men [ 42 ]. The authors found 24% lower risk for long-term light drinking (median intake ∼2.5 g/day) (HR 0.76; 95% CI 0.61–0.95) and 39% lower risk for moderate drinking (median intake ∼20 g/day) (HR 0.61; 95% CI 0.46–0.81) with all-cause mortality ( n = 568 total deaths); no evidence of increased mortality for heavy drinking (median intake ∼59 g/day) was observed (HR 0.95; 95% CI 0.63–1.43) [ 42 ]. While the authors acknowledge the limited availability of data on confounders, mediators of the alcohol–mortality association may also have been included in the models [ 42 ]. Our analysis is also not immune from other biases seen in observational studies that potentially overestimate the size of any health benefits arising from light to moderate drinking [ 43 ], although the use of drinking trajectories limits the contamination of the reference abstainer category by former heavy drinkers. The World Health Organization’s latest expert summary states that no safe amount of alcohol consumption can be established [ 11 ]. Any longevity benefit of light to moderate drinking at an individual level is complex and intertwined with distinct life circumstances and personal medical histories [ 9 ]. While there is no consensus on the health benefits of light to moderate drinking [ 11 ], it is widely recognized that people who do not consume alcohol should remain non-drinkers [ 40 ], as even low intakes have been shown to be associated with increased cancer risk [ 44–46 ].

In summary, we highlight the importance of avoiding higher levels of alcohol intake at any age to reduce all-cause and cancer-specific mortality. Prospective studies with similar data should aim to replicate these analyses.
